column4: The tree rising from Mount Sinai and producing oil and food places the olive itself on the mountain, exactly enacting the section's fruit-to-place reading of the oath.
This is the Quran's other explicit oath by the Mount, so it directly confirms that Tūr can stand as a sworn place.
Moses notices a fire at the side of the Mount; the verb ءَانَسَ is the section's named lexical bridge from seeing the fire to ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ.
The call comes from a tree in the blessed patch on the right bank of the valley, making the Mount a precisely located meeting of tree, blessing, and revelation.
At the same encounter Moses recoils in fear and is told that he is among the secure, giving the section its concrete passage from fear to safety at Tūr.
God calls Moses from the Mount's right side and brings him near for intimate speech; that nearness also answers the section's secondary contrast between بعد and proximity.
The Prophet is told that he was not beside the Mount when God called, preserving both the exact place of revelation and the revelation-based stance from which he can recount it.
The right side of the Mount is simultaneously Israel's appointed meeting place and the setting of manna and quail, joining covenantal place with provision.
God takes Israel's covenant and raises the Mount above them while commanding them to hold fast to what was given, directly making Tūr a place and sign of the covenant.
This repeated raising of the Mount accompanies the covenant and the command to hear and obey, sharpening the section's association of the mountain with pledged obedience.
The Mount is raised over Israel for their covenant in an ayah that also gives commands concerning the gate and Sabbath, tying the place to binding limits.
The mountain is lifted over the people like a canopy and they think it will fall, turning covenantal proximity to the mountain into palpable fear and compelled attention.
Abraham's prayer, “make this city secure,” directly supplies the prayer behind “this secure city” and keeps its deictic “this.”
Abraham locates his descendants in an uncultivated valley beside the Sacred House and asks for hearts and fruits to come to them, joining residence, House, worship, and provision.
The House is made a recurring destination and a security for people, while its circumambulators and residents echo the section's secondary images of circling, approaching, and staying at a dwelling.
Abraham asks that this become a secure town and that its inhabitants receive fruits, bringing the oath's fruit and secure-place images into one prayer.
The first House established for humanity is identified at Bakkah as blessed and guiding, supplying the named sacred center within the sworn city.
The ayah says that whoever enters the House is safe and makes pilgrimage to it a duty for one able to find a way, joining entry, security, and movement toward the center.
The Prophet is commanded to worship the Lord of “this city,” the One who made it sacred; the speaker's location and the city's protected status match the section exactly.
A secure sanctuary is set against people being snatched away all around it, and belief in falsehood against denial of God's blessing; this is the section's center-and-periphery contrast in one ayah.
The objection that guidance would lead to being snatched from the land is answered by a secure sanctuary to which fruits of every kind are gathered, uniting fear, safety, place, and fruit.
The command to worship the Lord of this House closely parallels the command to worship the Lord of this city in 27:91.
The Lord of the House provides food against hunger and security against fear, stating the section's definition of security through its opposite and linking it to provision.
The oath by “this city” is the explicit structural counterpart to the same deictic city oath in surah 95.
The Prophet's presence in this city makes the deictic oath local and inhabited, just as the section says “this” places the hearer inside the city.
After the city oath, this surah declares the human created in hardship, directly complementing surah 95's declaration that the human was created in the finest form.
A town is secure and tranquil with provision arriving abundantly, then tastes hunger and fear for ingratitude; it is a full reversal of the secure city's blessing and the denial named in 29:67.
The promised entry into the Sacred Mosque is explicitly “in security” and “without fear,” so movement across its boundary culminates in the same safety the section assigns to the House.
The believers once feared being snatched away, then God sheltered and provided for them, closely restaging the danger outside the sanctuary and the gifts of safety and provision inside it.
The Kaaba, the Sacred House, is made a sustaining institution for people together with sacred times and offerings, developing the House as an ordered human center.
The Sacred Mosque is equally open to the resident and the visitor, while deviation within it is threatened; the ayah defines both habitation at the center and the moral force of its boundary.
God assigns Abraham the site of the House and commands its purification for those who circle, stand, bow, and prostrate, joining place-making with approach and worship.
Pilgrims come to the House on foot and by mount from every distant pass, answering the section's contrasts of house and journey, near and far.
The pilgrims complete their rites and circle the Ancient House, giving the House's recurring return and the section's image of circling a concrete act.
A blessed Book warns the Mother of Cities and those around it, combining revelation with a sacred urban center and a named surrounding region.
Arabic revelation is sent to warn the Mother of Cities and those around it, and the same ayah points to the Day of Gathering; city, revelation, and judgment meet explicitly.
God restrains both sides' hands within Mecca after granting advantage, showing the named city's sacred boundary operating amid threatened violence.
Those who bar access to the Sacred Mosque also hold back the offerings, while unknown believers within Mecca constrain violence; the ayah makes the sanctuary's protected human interior concrete.
Moses comes to God's appointed time, God speaks to him, and the mountain is crushed by the manifestation; revelation, meeting, fear, and mountain are staged together.
The declaration that God spoke directly to Moses states the distinctive divine-human speech that the section locates at Tūr.
Moses tells his family to wait after he notices a fire and hopes to bring a brand or guidance from it, repeating the ءَانَسَ fire scene named in the section.
When Moses reaches the fire he is called by name, marking the perceived fire as the threshold of direct address.
The caller identifies Himself as Moses' Lord and names the setting as the sacred valley of Ṭuwā, specifying the sanctity of the mountain encounter.
God says He has chosen Moses and commands him to listen to the revelation, making the encounter an act of selection and transmission.
Within the revelation at the sacred valley, God announces the coming Hour and recompense for every soul, directly joining the Mount's revelation to the dīn toward which surah 95 moves.
Moses notices a fire, leaves his family waiting, and seeks news or a burning brand, a second Quranic formulation of the exact ءَانَسَ scene.
At the fire Moses is called and blessing is declared upon whoever is at it and around it, making the surrounding place itself part of the sacred encounter.
The voice identifies the speaker as God, the Mighty and Wise, specifying whose call makes the place revelatory.
Moses turns away in fear from the moving staff and is told not to fear because messengers do not fear in God's presence, repeating the encounter's fear-to-safety turn.
God's call to Moses is located in the sacred valley of Ṭuwā, independently confirming the place of revelation.
The thirty-night appointment with Moses is completed by ten, and Moses leaves Aaron responsible for his people; the ayah supplies the appointed meeting that Tūr signifies.
A mountain would humble and split from fear if the Quran descended upon it, illuminating why a mountain that bears revelation and covenant can become an oath-sign.
The light parable centers a blessed olive tree whose oil nearly shines, linking the oath's olive and Sinai's oil-bearing tree to fire-like light and blessing.
Immediately before the Sinai tree, gardens of palms and grapes supply abundant fruit to eat; this row contributes the provision scene from which 23:20 singles out the mountain tree.
The oath by the Mount immediately continues with an inscribed Book, making written revelation the first object placed beside Tūr.
The oath sequence moves from the Mount and Book to the frequented House, closely paralleling the section's movement from mountain revelation toward a House-centered city.
The answer to the Mount's oath is that the Lord's punishment will occur, so this other Tūr oath also presses toward the certainty of judgment.
Abraham asks which side has the greater right to security, directly making الأمن a theological question rather than merely a feature of geography.
The answer gives security to those who believe without clothing their faith in wrongdoing, bringing the shared ءمن family of belief and security into an explicit claim.
God promises believers who do right that He will replace their fear with security as they worship Him, joining faith, righteous action, rule, and the fear-security reversal.
A protected outsider is to hear God's speech and then be escorted to his مَأْمَنه, the very safe-place form named in the section's dictionary note.
Visible settlements, measured stages of travel, and safe journey by night or day unite bounded habitation, distance, movement, and security.
Entry into houses other than one's own requires تَسْتَأْنِسُوا and greeting their people, concretely placing “familiarity” at the boundary of an inhabited home.
If no one is found in a house, entry is forbidden without permission and a visitor told to return must return, specifying how absence and habitation change a dwelling's boundary.
Rules for entering and leaving the Prophet's houses culminate in the prohibition on lingering مُسْتَأْنِسِينَ in conversation, joining the ءنس sense of sociability to domestic limits.
The command not to approach God's limits gives a direct Quranic counterpart to the section's images of approaching a court and respecting a boundary.
God's limits must not be transgressed, directly restating the section's secondary Tūr image of going beyond one's assigned bound.
Women are not to be expelled from their houses nor leave them in the prescribed period, and this domestic rule is named among God's limits; house, staying, and boundary coincide.
Joseph could not have taken his brother under the king's دِين unless God willed, supplying the rule-and-obedience sense of dīn behind the section's etymological note on “city.”
Belief and righteous action lead to multiplied reward in elevated chambers where their occupants are secure, joining the section's صلح and ءمن threads in an inhabited reward-place.
Thamūd are settled in the land, building palaces on plains and carving homes in mountains, a direct Quranic meeting of habitation, bounded human space, and mountain.
God makes houses places of rest and animal-skin tents light for days of travel and days of residence, precisely staging home, mobility, and staying.
God makes shelters in the mountains alongside other forms of protection, showing security extending beyond the city into the mountainous outside.
The God-conscious are placed in a مَقَامٍ أَمِينٍ, extending the image of a secure inhabited place from the earthly city to the final abode.
In that secure abode they call for every fruit while safe, reuniting the oath's fruit and secure-place images in the hereafter.
Joseph tells his family to enter Egypt, God willing, secure; an act of entry and family resettlement gives safety a geographic form beyond the sanctuary.
The command to enter the gardens in peace and security makes safe entry the mark of the final dwelling, a clear eschatological extension of entering the House safely.
After the provision at the Mount, Israel is told to eat the good things and not exceed bounds in them lest wrath descend; covenantal provision is explicitly enclosed by a limit.
The Prophet was not on the western side when the command was decreed to Moses and was not a witness, contributing the same spatial absence that 28:46 specifies as the Mount.
Moses is told to draw in his arm against fear as he receives the two signs, continuing the bodily transition from alarm to reassurance begun in 28:31.
When Moses and Aaron fear Pharaoh's violence, God tells them not to fear because He is with them hearing and seeing, another divine assurance to Moses grounded in presence.
God's forty-night appointment with Moses is the repeated covenantal meeting later localized at the right side of Tūr.
The giving of the Book and criterion to Moses states the revelatory gift associated with that appointment and mountain.
Manna and quail are sent down to Israel as good provision, repeating the food named beside the Mount in 20:80.
The cloud, manna, and quail provide Israel shade and food, another concrete version of the provision recalled at the right side of Tūr.
The oath by parent and offspring carries the city oath toward 90:4's created human, supplying the generational hinge inside the parallel structure.
Ṣafā and Marwah are sacred waymarks traversed by one visiting the House, bringing hill, movement, and sanctuary into one ritual geography.
The command to walk through the earth's pathways, eat God's provision, and remember the resurrection opposes blameworthy confinement at home with purposeful movement toward judgment.

The command to travel through the land and observe how creation began leads directly to the final creation, matching the section's house-leaving motif and surah 95's move from human creation to judgment.
Animals carry burdens to a town that people could reach only with great hardship, making a settlement the goal of difficult travel across distance.
Sheba is called a good town with gardens, provision, and a forgiving Lord, a close positive counterpart to the fruitful secure city.
The people of al-Ḥijr carve houses from mountains while feeling secure; their coming destruction exposes the limit of treating mountain dwellings as guaranteed safety.
The morning blast seizes the people who had felt secure in their mountain houses, completing the reversal stated in 15:82.
The people are asked whether they expect to be left secure in their cultivated surroundings, challenging confidence in a settled place.
Their carving of houses from mountains supplies the physical basis of that confidence, while the passage turns it into a warning rather than a promise of safety.
People who thought their fortresses would protect them are expelled from their homes as fear enters their hearts, directly reversing homebound confidence in enclosed space.
Immediately after the secure-sanctuary claim, ruined towns are shown through dwellings scarcely inhabited afterward; a place defined by settlement becomes almost empty.
When Sheba turns away, its two fruitful gardens are replaced by bitter and sparse growth, reversing the provision of the good town in 34:15.
The loss is named as recompense for ingratitude, matching the section's warning that denying a place's blessing has consequences.
The people ask that the distances between their journeys be lengthened and their settled route is scattered, turning the measured safe travel of 34:18 into dislocation.
The ayah contrasts one cast into the Fire with one who comes secure on Resurrection Day, setting final security against judgment rather than locating it in an earthly boundary.
No one can feel secure from the Lord's punishment, marking the ultimate boundary of every local or worldly claim to safety.
Satan and his kind see human beings from where humans do not see them, giving a Quranic form to the section's visible-human versus unseen-being distinction.
Jinn and humankind are challenged to pass beyond the regions of heaven and earth but cannot without authority, joining the named human-jinn pair to a limit that cannot simply be crossed.
The youths withdraw from their people into a cave and seek mercy and right guidance there, reversing the expectation that safety must lie inside the inhabited city.
Their dog lies with forelegs stretched at the cave entrance while the hidden youths inspire flight and terror, placing the section's domestic-dog image at the threshold of a wild refuge.
The youths explain that discovery by the city's people would mean stoning or forced apostasy, specifying why the populated city is dangerous and the cave protective.
A pilgrim in consecration may not kill land game, so the sacred state places a legal boundary around pursuit of the wild animal named in the section's secondary image.
Sea game is permitted while land game remains forbidden during consecration, making the boundary around wild creatures explicit through a paired ruling.
Rain is driven to a dead بَلَد and brings out fruits; the same word used for inhabited city can name lifeless land awaiting revival.
Winds and clouds revive a dead بَلَد, and the ayah likens that revival to resurrection, connecting the word's uninhabited sense to the section's turn toward judgment.
Measured water revives a dead بَلْدَة and becomes an analogy for being brought forth, again setting lifeless land against the inhabited secure city.
Rain revives a dead بَلْدَة as provision for servants and an image of emergence from death, joining place, provision, and return.
The question “Has the account of Moses reached you?” introduces the sacred-valley call in 79:16 and shares the revelatory stance of recounting an event the listener did not witness.
God's call to Moses and commission to the wrongdoing people is another formulation of the speech that begins at the mountain encounter, though this ayah does not name its place.
Moses and Aaron voice fear that Pharaoh may act violently, supplying the danger to which God's reassurance in 20:46 responds.
A man comes running from the farthest part of the city to warn Moses that the ruling council plans to kill him, combining the city's edge, authority, and impending departure.
Moses leaves the city fearful and watchful while praying for rescue, a reversal of the secure-city image within the life of the same prophet met at Tūr.
After Moses reaches Midian, the elder tells him not to fear because he has escaped the wrongdoing people, completing another movement from city-borne fear to safety.
From their hidden refuge the youths send one companion cautiously into the city to buy pure food, sharply staging movement between wilderness shelter and inhabited marketplace.
Abraham places portions of birds on mountains and calls them back, a concrete Quranic meeting of wild birds, mountains, approach, and resurrection rather than a lexical use of Tūr.
Solomon's forces of jinn, humans, and birds are gathered and kept in ordered ranks, countering the section's wild-beyond-the-boundary image with disciplined assembly.
The night journey moves from the Sacred Mosque to the farther mosque whose surroundings are blessed, providing another revelation-centered passage between sacred places.
The hypocrites would follow for a near gain and easy journey, but the distance is too great for them; the ayah gives the section's near-far and house-leaving contrast a concrete journey.
A messenger says he has warned everyone equally but does not know whether the promised event is near or far, joining the بعد–proximity contrast to promised judgment.
Reports of security or fear are set as opposites and must be referred to proper authority, directly reflecting the dictionary definition while adding the problem of civic discernment.
“Is God not sufficient for His servant?” is followed by people trying to frighten the Prophet, so the أَلَيْسَ stance becomes an assurance against fear.
After 29:67 contrasts the secure sanctuary with belief in falsehood, this ayah names fabricating falsehood and denying truth, then asks with أَلَيْسَ about the unbelievers' lodging in Hell.
The closing question أَلَيْسَ asks whether the Creator can revive the dead, closely matching surah 95's final rhetorical appeal from creation to judgment.

The hypocrites imagine that on returning to Medina the stronger will expel the weaker, exposing a false claim to civic rule within the very place whose name the section links to authority and obedience.
